reading.title: Reading mini-test 5: A Saturday at the Market
paragraphs: A. Every Saturday, Dilnoza goes to the big market in her town with her mother. They leave home at seven in the morning because the market is busy after nine. They go by bus, and the ride takes about twenty minutes.

B. First, they buy vegetables and fruit. Dilnoza likes red apples and sweet grapes, but her mother always buys tomatoes and onions first. The prices are lower at the market than in the supermarket, so many families shop there.

C. Next, they visit the bread section. A man called Rustam sells fresh bread from a traditional oven. He starts baking at five o’clock, and by eight the best bread is usually finished. Dilnoza always eats a small piece while it is still hot.

D. At eleven o’clock, they have tea and a snack at a small cafe near the entrance. Then they carry the heavy bags to the bus stop. Dilnoza is tired when she gets home, but she says the market is the best part of her week.

reading.title: Reading mini-test 1: The Rise of the Rooftop Garden
reading.passageTitle: The Rise of the Rooftop Garden
paragraphs: A. In many large cities, the tops of buildings are among the least used spaces. For most of the twentieth century, roofs were treated as simple coverings, designed to keep rain out and little else. In recent decades, however, architects and city planners have begun to see them as an opportunity. Rooftop gardens, once a rare luxury found on a handful of hotels and private homes, are now appearing on schools, hospitals and office blocks around the world.

B. One of the main reasons for this change is heat. Cities are usually warmer than the surrounding countryside, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. Dark surfaces such as asphalt and tar roofing absorb sunlight during the day and release it slowly at night. One study of a North American city suggested that if all suitable roofs were covered with plants, the average summer temperature in the centre could fall by up to two degrees Celsius. On a single building, a green roof can also reduce the cost of cooling the rooms below, because the layer of soil and plants acts as insulation.

C. Water management is a second benefit. In a city, rain that falls on hard surfaces runs quickly into drains, and during heavy storms the drainage system can be overwhelmed, causing floods. A green roof absorbs part of this rainfall and releases it slowly. Studies in several European countries have suggested that a roof with a soil layer of about ten centimetres can keep around half of the yearly rainfall from reaching the drains at all.

D. Rooftop gardens are not only practical. They also create habitats for wildlife. In cities where parks are small and far apart, insects and birds can use roofs as stepping stones between green areas. Some enthusiasts have gone further and placed beehives on rooftops, and honey produced in the middle of a city is now sold in several markets as a local speciality.

E. There are, however, challenges. A green roof is much heavier than a conventional one, so the building must be strong enough to carry the extra load, especially when the soil is wet. Installation typically costs two to three times as much as a normal roof, and the plants need regular watering and weeding. Yet over time the plant layer protects the waterproof membrane from sunlight and sudden changes in temperature. As a result, a green roof may last around forty years, compared with about twenty for a conventional roof.

F. Governments have started to respond. A few cities now require new large buildings with flat roofs to include vegetation, while others simply offer tax reductions to owners who install green roofs. Critics argue that rules which demand plants may be less effective than rules which set targets for cooling or water retention, leaving builders free to choose the best method for each building.

reading.title: Reading mini-test 6: Why More People Are Cycling to Work
reading.passageTitle: Why More People Are Cycling to Work
paragraphs: A. In many cities, the number of people who cycle to work has grown steadily over the last ten years. Some workers say that the main reason is cost. A monthly bus ticket can be expensive, while a bicycle needs only a small amount of money for repairs.

B. Health is another reason. Doctors recommend at least thirty minutes of exercise a day, and many office workers find it difficult to fit that into a busy schedule. Cycling to work solves the problem, because the journey itself becomes exercise. One survey found that cyclists took fewer days off sick than people who drove.

C. However, cycling is not always easy. In cities without separate bicycle lanes, riders share the road with cars and buses, and many people feel unsafe. Bad weather is also a problem: few people enjoy arriving at the office wet and cold.

D. To help, some companies now provide showers and secure places to keep bicycles. A few offer small payments to employees who cycle. City councils are also building new lanes, although progress is often slow because the work is expensive.

reading.title: Reading mini-test 9: The Return of the Bicycle Courier
reading.passageTitle: The Return of the Bicycle Courier
paragraphs: A. Ten years ago, most parcels in large cities were delivered by van. Today, more and more of them arrive by bicycle. Delivery companies say that bikes are often faster than vans in busy city centres, because they can use cycle lanes and do not need to look for parking spaces.

B. Many of the new bikes are cargo bikes, which have a large box at the front or back. Some of them have a small electric motor, so riders can carry up to one hundred kilograms without becoming exhausted. A cargo bike costs much less than a van, and it does not need fuel.

C. City councils are also interested. Fewer vans on the roads means less traffic and cleaner air. Some cities have created special areas where companies can leave large deliveries; from there, the parcels are taken to their final address by bike. This system is often called “the last mile”.

D. However, the job is not easy. Couriers work outside in all weather, and in winter the roads can be dangerous. Many of them are paid for each delivery rather than for each hour, so a slow day means low earnings. Some couriers have started to ask companies for better pay and insurance.

E. Experts believe the number of bicycle deliveries will keep growing, especially as online shopping becomes more popular. But they also say that bikes cannot replace vans completely: large or very heavy items, such as furniture, will still need to travel by road.

reading.title: Reading mini-test 10: Why We Trust Strangers Online
paragraphs: A. Every day, millions of people book rooms in the homes of people they have never met, or buy expensive second-hand items from strangers hundreds of kilometres away. A generation ago, most of these transactions would have seemed far too risky. What has changed is not human nature but the arrival of systems designed to build trust between people who will probably never meet again.

B. The most familiar of these systems is the rating. After a transaction, both sides give each other a score and often a short written review. Over time, these scores form a public record. Researchers have found that people are strongly influenced by the first few reviews they read, and that a single very negative comment can outweigh several positive ones.

C. Ratings have obvious weaknesses, however. Because many users feel awkward about criticising someone directly, average scores on some platforms are extremely high, which makes it difficult to tell an excellent seller from an ordinary one. In addition, some businesses pay for fake positive reviews, and platforms must spend considerable effort detecting them.

D. Platforms therefore combine ratings with other signals. Verified identity documents, connected phone numbers and secure payment systems all reduce the risk that a user is not who they claim to be. Some platforms hold the buyer’s money until the item has arrived in good condition, so that neither side has to take the first step on trust alone.

E. Interestingly, studies suggest that people trust online strangers who appear similar to themselves, for example in age or interests, more than those who seem different. Critics warn that this tendency can disadvantage certain groups, and some platforms have reduced the amount of personal information shown before a booking is confirmed.

reading.title: Reading mini-test 3: The Return of the Night Train
reading.passageTitle: The Return of the Night Train
paragraphs: A. Thirty years ago, an overnight train journey was a normal way to cross Europe. Then budget airlines arrived. With tickets sometimes costing less than a train sandwich, many routes lost passengers, and railway companies cancelled their night services one after another. By the early 2010s, only a handful of sleeper trains were left on the continent.

B. Recently, the picture has begun to change. Growing concern about climate change has led many travellers to look for ways to reduce their carbon footprint, and some now choose not to fly when an alternative exists. Several governments have responded by supporting new night routes, and passenger numbers on the restored services have often been higher than expected.

C. Night trains have clear advantages. Passengers travel from one city centre to another, avoiding long journeys to and from airports. Tickets are not always cheaper than flights, but travellers save the cost of a hotel room, since they sleep on the train. Emissions per passenger are also much lower than on a plane.

D. There are, however, practical problems. Many sleeper carriages are old and uncomfortable, and few factories still build new ones. International journeys are complicated by technical differences: countries use different power systems and signals, so locomotives and drivers often have to change at the border. In addition, companies must pay fees for using the tracks, and night services compete for space with freight trains.

E. Operators are trying to solve the comfort problem. New sleeper cars offer private cabins with their own washbasins and showers, and some companies have ordered dozens of them. Better design, supporters argue, can turn the night train from a cheap necessity into a pleasant experience.

F. Most analysts do not expect trains to replace aeroplanes on very long routes. But on journeys of up to about twelve hours, a night train can leave in the evening and arrive in the morning, and that makes it a realistic competitor. If more investment follows, the sleeper train may become a permanent part of European travel once again.

reading.title: Reading mini-test 4: Learning a Language as an Adult
reading.passageTitle: Learning a Language as an Adult
paragraphs: A. Many adults believe that it is too late to learn a foreign language. Research suggests otherwise. In the first months of study, adults often learn grammar rules faster than children, because they can use logic and their knowledge of their own language. Children, on the other hand, usually develop a more natural accent. The two groups simply have different strengths.

B. Motivation matters a great deal. Adults who have a clear goal, such as a new job or a plan to move abroad, tend to keep studying even when progress slows. Those who learn only because they feel they should often give up within weeks. Many teachers therefore begin by asking students what exactly they want to do with the language.

C. Method matters too. One study followed two hundred adult learners for a year. Those who began speaking in the first week, even with simple sentences, progressed faster than those who waited until they felt ready. Spaced repetition, in which words are reviewed at increasing intervals, also helped learners remember vocabulary for longer.

D. Adults face barriers that children do not. Most are short of time, and many are afraid of making mistakes in front of others. Classes where a teacher gives regular, friendly feedback can reduce this fear, and learners in such classes are more likely to continue.

E. Finally, there may be wider benefits. Some researchers believe that people who speak two languages show signs of memory decline later in life, but the evidence is not yet conclusive. What is clear is that learners often report greater confidence and new friendships.

reading.title: Reading mini-test 2: The Hidden Work of Sleep
paragraphs: A. For centuries, sleep was seen as a passive state, a kind of switching off that the body needed in order to recover. Modern research has shown the opposite. Brain scans reveal that during the night the brain passes through several cycles, and in some of them it is almost as active as when we are awake. Far from being idle, the sleeping brain is busy with tasks that cannot be done during the day.

B. One of these tasks is memory. During deep sleep the brain replays the events of the day, moving information from short-term memory to long-term storage. In one experiment, two groups of students studied the same list of words. The group that slept after studying remembered considerably more words the next morning than the group that stayed awake. Sleep, it seems, does not just preserve what we learn; it makes it stronger.

C. The body also uses the night to repair itself. Growth hormone is released mostly during deep sleep, helping muscles and tissues to recover. The immune system is active too: people who regularly sleep for fewer than six hours are more likely to catch a cold than those who sleep for eight. Doctors now regard sleep as one of the basic protections for health, alongside food and exercise.

D. Teenagers face a particular problem. During puberty the body clock shifts, so that young people naturally feel sleepy later in the evening and wake later in the morning. Yet most schools begin early. When some schools moved the start of lessons back by one hour, attendance improved, students reported better moods, and the number of road accidents involving young drivers fell.

E. Modern life makes good sleep harder. Artificial light in the evening, and especially the blue light from phones and tablets, delays the release of melatonin, the hormone that tells the body it is time to sleep. Experts advise keeping a regular schedule, sleeping in a dark room and avoiding screens for an hour before bed.

F. However, sleep is not the same for everyone. Most adults need between seven and nine hours, but some people function well on slightly less, and others need more. Sleeping late at weekends can reduce the effects of a short week, but it only partly makes up for lost sleep. Researchers stress that regular, sufficient sleep cannot simply be stored up or caught up later.

reading.passageTitle: Reading Passage 1: The Quiet Revolution of the Bicycle
paragraphs: A. Few machines have changed everyday life as quietly as the bicycle. Its story begins in 1817, when the German inventor Karl Drais built a two-wheeled “running machine”. It had no pedals: the rider sat on a wooden frame and pushed against the ground with both feet. Drais hoped it would offer an alternative to the horse, but the machine was heavy, uncomfortable and difficult to steer on rough roads, and interest soon faded. At the time, travel over land depended almost entirely on animals or on walking, and the roads between towns were often little more than tracks of mud or stone. Drais demonstrated his invention by covering around thirteen kilometres in less than an hour, faster than a walking pace, and copies were soon made in several countries. In cities, however, riders were accused of frightening pedestrians on the pavements, and some authorities introduced rules against riding there.

B. Pedals appeared several decades later, when makers in France attached cranks directly to the front wheel. Because each turn of the pedals produced only one turn of that wheel, designers who wanted more speed simply made the front wheel larger. The result was the high-wheeled machine of the 1870s, later nicknamed the “penny-farthing”. It was fast, but the rider sat high above the ground, and a sudden stop could throw him over the handlebars. Riding it was regarded as a sport for brave young men rather than a practical form of transport. Its large front wheel did have one practical advantage on poor roads: it rolled more easily over holes and stones, so the ride was less rough than on a machine with small wheels. Clubs were formed in which members rode together, organised races and published magazines about their hobby. Because the machines were expensive as well as dangerous, however, they remained the possessions of a fairly small group, and the general public tended to see them as a curiosity.

C. The decisive change came in the 1880s with the so-called safety bicycle. It had two wheels of similar size and a chain that carried power from the pedals to the rear wheel. Gearing meant that speed no longer depended on wheel size, so the rider could sit lower and put a foot on the ground. Soon afterwards, the air-filled tyre, developed by John Boyd Dunlop in 1888, made journeys far smoother than solid rubber had allowed. Manufacturers quickly saw the commercial possibilities. Factories began to produce standard parts, such as steel tubes, ball bearings and spokes, in large numbers, which made bicycles lighter and more reliable. Within a few years, the new design had replaced the high-wheeler almost completely. Its basic shape — a diamond-shaped frame, two equal wheels and a chain drive — has changed remarkably little since then, and most bicycles sold today would be easily recognised by a rider from the 1890s.

D. The social effects were remarkable. In the 1890s, cycling became a craze in Europe and North America. For the first time, many working people could travel several kilometres to a job without paying for a train or keeping a horse. The bicycle also gave women a new independence of movement, and the fashion for long, heavy skirts began to change because they were impractical for riding. Cycling clubs organised weekend trips into the countryside, and new maps and guidebooks were printed for riders. Doctors and writers argued about whether the activity was healthy, with some warning of exhaustion and others praising the benefits of fresh air and exercise. The industries that grew up around the bicycle also had a longer influence: several of the engineers and companies that made bicycles later applied their skills to building motor cars and even early aeroplanes.

E. During the twentieth century, cars pushed bicycles to the side of many roads, especially in wealthy countries. Yet the machine never disappeared. In several cities, planners have recently built separate lanes and parking for bicycles, arguing that they reduce traffic and improve public health. Today, electric bicycles, which add a small motor to the rider’s own effort, are introducing cycling to people who once thought hills or long distances made it impossible. In some countries, such as the Netherlands and Denmark, cycling has remained a normal way for people of all ages to travel to work or school, supported by decades of investment in infrastructure that keeps riders apart from motor traffic. Elsewhere, bicycle-sharing schemes allow people to hire a bicycle for a short journey and leave it at another station.

F. Researchers who study transport point out that the bicycle remains one of the most energy-efficient ways of moving a person ever devised. A cyclist uses less energy per kilometre than a person walking, and a bicycle requires only a small fraction of the materials and road space needed for a car. For these reasons, many planners see it not as a relic of the nineteenth century but as part of the answer to modern problems of congestion and pollution. Two centuries after Drais pushed his wooden machine along the road, the simple idea of balancing on two wheels is still developing.

A. Most people are familiar with the experience of studying something carefully, only to find a week later that much of it has gone. In the 1880s, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus tried to measure this loss. Using himself as the only subject, he memorised lists of meaningless syllables and tested how many he could recall after different intervals. His results suggested that forgetting is fastest soon after learning and then slows down, a pattern now known as the forgetting curve. Ebbinghaus chose nonsense syllables, made of a consonant, a vowel and another consonant, because real words carry meanings and associations that could make some items easier to remember than others. He repeated his experiments over several years and recorded his results with great care. Although his method had obvious limitations — he was studying only one person, and an unusually disciplined one — many of his findings have since been confirmed by studies with large groups of participants.

B. Later research has shown that the curve is not fixed. One of the most reliable findings in psychology is the spacing effect: material that is reviewed several times, with gaps between the sessions, is remembered far longer than material studied for the same total time in a single block. Cramming the night before an examination may produce a reasonable score the next morning, but most of what was learned disappears soon afterwards. The size of the benefit depends partly on the length of the gaps. In general, the longer something needs to be remembered, the longer the intervals between reviews should be. A student preparing for an examination in a month might review new material after a day, then after a few days, and again after a week or two. Each review takes less time than the one before, because less has been forgotten in between.

C. A second powerful technique is retrieval practice. When learners try to recall information without looking at it — for example, by answering questions or writing down everything they remember — they strengthen the memory more than when they simply reread their notes. Rereading feels productive because the material looks familiar, but familiarity is not the same as being able to produce the information when it is needed. In one well-known type of experiment, two groups read the same short text. One group then reads it again several times, while the other reads it once and spends the remaining time writing down what it can recall. When tested a few minutes later, the rereading group often performs slightly better; when tested a week later, however, the group that practised recalling remembers considerably more.

D. Why should effortful recall be so effective? One explanation is that each successful retrieval makes the route to a memory easier to find next time. Another is that recall shows learners which parts they have not yet mastered, so they can direct their attention there. Interestingly, researchers have found that a failed attempt to remember, if it is followed by the correct answer, can still improve later recall. Some researchers also believe that retrieval links a memory to more cues and contexts, so that it can be reached in a greater variety of situations. Whatever the exact mechanism, the practical lesson is that some difficulty during learning is useful. Psychologists have described such helpful challenges as “desirable difficulties”: they slow learning down at first but lead to stronger and longer-lasting results.

E. Sleep also plays an important part. Studies in which people learn new material in the evening and are tested the following morning suggest that a night of sleep helps to stabilise what has been learned. Students who give up sleep to study longer may therefore weaken the very memories they are trying to build. During deep sleep, the brain appears to replay patterns of activity from the day, and this may help to transfer new information into longer-term storage. Even a short daytime nap has been linked in some studies to better memory for material learned shortly before it. The effect seems to be strongest for information that the learner expects to need again later.

F. None of these findings is new, yet they are often ignored. Many students continue to highlight, reread and cram, partly because these methods feel easier. Some teachers now build short, low-pressure quizzes into their lessons and return to earlier topics weeks later. The aim is not to test students more, but to turn remembering itself into a way of learning. One reason is that the benefits of good methods are delayed, while their costs are felt immediately: spaced review and self-testing feel slower and more frustrating than a final night of intensive study. Surveys of university students in several countries have found that rereading is the most popular strategy, even among those who have heard of more effective ones. Changing these habits may require not only information but also study plans that make the better methods easier to follow.

A. On a summer afternoon, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the countryside around it. This difference, called the urban heat island effect, has been observed in cities on every continent. It is usually strongest at night, when the surrounding fields cool quickly while streets and buildings go on releasing the heat they absorbed during the day. The phenomenon was described long before it had a name: in the early nineteenth century, an amateur scientist in London recorded that the city was noticeably warmer than the surrounding countryside. The size of the difference depends on the size of the city, the weather and the season, and it is greatest on calm, clear nights, when there is little wind to mix warm and cool air.

B. Several features of cities produce the effect. Dark surfaces such as asphalt roads and roofs absorb a large share of the sunlight that falls on them. Concrete and brick store this heat and release it slowly. In addition, cities have fewer trees and less open soil, so less water evaporates — a process that naturally cools the air. Heat from vehicles, factories and air conditioners adds a further, smaller contribution. The form of the city matters too. Where tall buildings stand close together, they can block the wind that would otherwise carry warm air away from the streets, and the heat absorbed by their walls during the day is released into the same narrow space at night. Measurements show that on a sunny afternoon the surface of a dark roof can be far hotter than the air above it, and this heat continues to warm the building and the street for hours after sunset.

C. The consequences are more than a matter of comfort. During heatwaves, high night-time temperatures prevent the body from recovering, and older people and those with health problems face the greatest risk. Hotter cities also use more electricity for cooling, which can place pressure on power networks at the moments of highest demand. The effect also influences air quality. Higher temperatures speed up the chemical reactions that produce ground-level ozone, a pollutant that irritates the lungs. Poorer neighbourhoods often have fewer trees and parks than wealthier ones, so their residents may experience higher temperatures and are also less likely to be able to afford air conditioning.

D. Some solutions are surprisingly simple. Painting roofs in light colours reflects more sunlight back into the sky, and so-called cool pavements use materials that stay cooler under the sun. Trees provide shade and release water vapour through their leaves, and parks of even modest size can be measurably cooler than the streets around them. Green roofs, covered with plants, insulate buildings and absorb rainwater as well as cooling the air. In several cities, authorities have set targets for increasing the share of land covered by trees, and some offer grants to property owners who paint their roofs white. Fountains, pools and small canals can also provide local cooling in squares and other public spaces.

E. However, none of these measures is a complete answer. Light-coloured surfaces can reflect sunlight onto nearby buildings and pedestrians, and trees need water, space and years of care before they offer much shade. In dry regions, planners must balance the cooling benefits of vegetation against the limited supply of water. Experts therefore tend to recommend a combination of measures chosen to suit each neighbourhood. Measuring the effect of each measure is also difficult, because temperatures vary greatly from one street to the next and from one day to another. For this reason, many cities now place networks of small sensors on lamp posts and buildings to record conditions in different districts.

F. Traditional architecture offers further ideas. In many hot countries, older districts were built with narrow streets that remain in shade for most of the day, thick walls that slow the movement of heat, and inner courtyards with plants or water. Some architects argue that these designs, developed over centuries, deserve as much attention as new technology. As summers become hotter, the question of how to keep cities cool is likely to become one of the central challenges of urban planning.

G. Climate change is likely to make the issue more urgent. As global temperatures rise, heatwaves are expected to become more frequent and more intense, and the extra warmth of cities will be added to this general increase. At the same time, the proportion of the world’s population living in urban areas continues to grow. Researchers stress that cooling cities will not solve the wider problem of climate change, but it can make the hottest days less dangerous for the people who have to live through them.

paragraphs: A. For most of its life, the desert locust is an unremarkable insect. It lives alone in the dry regions of North Africa, the Middle East and South Asia, avoiding other locusts and feeding on whatever sparse vegetation it can find. In this solitary phase it is green or brown, moves mainly at night and rarely travels far. Farmers in these regions may not even notice it. Desert locusts belong to the grasshopper family, and in their solitary form they look much like many of their harmless relatives. Their life cycle has three stages: egg, hopper (the wingless young insect) and winged adult, and in good conditions it takes about two to four months to complete. Because the regions where they live receive very little rain, the population usually stays small and scattered for years at a time.

B. Everything changes after heavy rain. Wet soil allows females to lay many more eggs, and fresh plants appear across the desert. As the vegetation later dries up and shrinks, the young locusts are pushed together into smaller and smaller areas. Researchers have found that repeated touching of the insects’ back legs triggers a remarkable transformation: within a few hours their behaviour changes, and over the following generations they become brightly coloured, more active and strongly attracted to one another. Scientists have identified a chemical messenger in the insects’ nervous system that appears to play a central role in this change. The transformation can also be reversed: if the insects become separated again, later generations gradually return to the solitary form. Laboratory experiments have shown that the change can be triggered simply by keeping many young locusts together in a small space, without any change in their food or temperature.

C. In this gregarious phase, locusts form bands of wingless young insects that march across the ground, and later swarms of adults that fly by day. A single swarm can cover several hundred square kilometres and contain billions of insects. Carried by the wind, swarms may travel well over a hundred kilometres in one day, and each insect can eat roughly its own weight in fresh food daily. Crops, pasture and trees can disappear in hours. Swarms usually land in the evening and settle on trees and bushes for the night before taking off again the next morning. A swarm of moderate size can consume as much food in one day as tens of thousands of people.

D. Major outbreaks have affected dozens of countries at once, threatening the food supply of millions of people. Because swarms cross borders so easily, no single country can deal with them alone. International organisations therefore collect reports from field teams, satellites and weather stations to identify areas where conditions favour breeding, often weeks before a swarm forms. Locust plagues have been recorded since ancient times and appear in the written records of several early civilisations. In the twentieth century, some plagues lasted for more than a decade. Today, national locust units in affected countries send survey teams into remote desert areas, where they record the number of insects and the state of the vegetation. This information is combined with weather data in computer models that forecast where swarms may develop next. Countries in the regions most often affected share their survey results through regional commissions, which also hold stocks of equipment that can be moved quickly to where it is needed.

E. The main method of control is still the spraying of chemical pesticides, usually from vehicles or aircraft. However, this approach is expensive and can harm other wildlife and people. Scientists have developed a biological alternative based on a natural fungus that infects only locusts and related insects. It works more slowly than chemicals, so it is most useful when outbreaks are detected early. Chemical treatment is most effective against hopper bands, which move slowly on the ground and can be targeted precisely, whereas flying swarms are much harder to hit. During large emergencies, millions of hectares may need to be treated, and the work is often slowed by conflict, poor roads and a shortage of trained staff in remote areas.

F. Climate is likely to make the problem harder to predict. Unusual cyclones and heavy rainfall over deserts can create ideal breeding conditions in places that are normally too dry. Experts argue that the best defence is not dramatic emergency spraying but steady, well-funded monitoring, so that small groups of locusts can be treated before they become swarms. Funding is a particular challenge. When no swarms appear for several years, governments and donors tend to move money to other priorities, and teams lose equipment and experience. When a major outbreak finally arrives, the response must then be rebuilt almost from the beginning, at much greater cost.

A. Parents often complain that teenagers stay up too late and cannot get out of bed in the morning. For a long time, this was seen simply as a question of discipline. Over the past few decades, however, sleep researchers have shown that the pattern has a strong biological basis. Teenagers who struggled to wake up were often described as lazy, and school timetables were planned around the needs of adults and younger children. Researchers began to question this view when laboratory studies, in which young people followed carefully controlled routines, showed that the timing of their sleep was shaped partly by changes inside the body.

B. Every person has an internal body clock that tells the body when to feel alert and when to feel sleepy. One of its signals is the hormone melatonin, which rises in the evening. During adolescence, the release of melatonin starts later at night, so many teenagers do not feel sleepy until around eleven o’clock or later. This shift appears in young people in many different countries, which suggests it is not just a result of modern lifestyles. The body clock is adjusted every day by signals from the environment and runs on a cycle of roughly twenty-four hours. In adolescence, the pressure to sleep also builds up more slowly during the day, so teenagers can stay awake comfortably for longer in the evening. The shift usually begins around puberty and reaches its latest point towards the end of the teenage years, after which sleep times gradually move earlier again.

C. At the same time, teenagers still need a great deal of sleep — about eight to ten hours a night, according to most health guidelines. If they fall asleep late and must wake early for school, they lose sleep every weekday. Many try to catch up at the weekend by sleeping until midday, but this can push their body clock even later, making Monday morning harder still. Scientists sometimes call this pattern “social jet lag”, because its effect is similar to flying across several time zones every weekend and back again on Monday. A teenager who sleeps from one in the morning until eleven on Saturday and Sunday, but from eleven at night until half past six during the week, is asking the body to adjust to a different schedule twice every seven days. Doctors therefore advise that wake-up times at the weekend should differ from those on school days by no more than an hour or two.

D. The effects of this lack of sleep are wide-ranging. Tired students find it harder to concentrate and remember what they have learned, and they are more likely to feel irritable or low. Research has also linked short sleep with a higher risk of road accidents among young drivers and with poorer decisions about food. Some studies have also found that students who sleep less tend to receive lower marks, although it is difficult to separate the effect of sleep from other factors, such as family circumstances or the amount of time spent on homework. In addition, long-term lack of sleep may weaken the body’s defences against common infections. Teachers in many countries report that the first lesson of the morning is often the most difficult, because many students appear to be only half awake.

E. Some school districts have responded by moving the start of the school day later, often by about an hour. Studies of these changes have generally found that students sleep longer, are absent less often and are less likely to fall asleep in class. Not everyone supports the idea, though: later starts can create difficulties for school bus timetables, after-school sports and parents’ working hours. Opponents also argue that the benefits may be lost if teenagers simply go to bed later as a result. Research so far suggests that this happens only to a small extent: most students whose school starts later still gain a significant amount of extra sleep each night.

F. Experts say that teenagers themselves can also make a difference. Bright light from phones and laptops late in the evening can delay sleep further, so they recommend switching off screens an hour before bed and keeping a similar bedtime on school days and at weekends. Getting daylight in the morning may also help to move the body clock earlier. Caffeine is another factor: energy drinks, coffee and strong tea in the afternoon or evening can make it harder to fall asleep. A regular routine before bed, such as reading or listening to quiet music, helps the body to recognise that it is time to rest. Experts stress, however, that individual changes can only go so far while lessons still begin early in the morning.

A. The five-day working week, with two days of rest, became standard in many countries during the twentieth century. Today, a growing number of companies are experimenting with a further change: a four-day week with no loss of pay. Supporters believe that shorter hours can make workers healthier and happier without reducing the amount they produce. The best-known version is sometimes called the “100-80-100” model: employees receive 100 per cent of their pay for 80 per cent of their previous hours, in return for a commitment to maintain 100 per cent of their output. Interest grew rapidly in the early 2020s, when many people had already experienced major changes to the way they worked.

B. The idea rests on a simple observation. In many office jobs, not every hour at work is productive; time is lost in unnecessary meetings, interruptions and slow processes. If staff know they have only four days to complete their work, the argument goes, they will find ways to remove these inefficiencies. Some managers report that teams became more focused and that the number of meetings fell sharply. Supporters also argue that rested employees make fewer mistakes and are more creative, because they return to work with more energy after a three-day weekend. Some companies prepared for their trials by reviewing every regular meeting, shortening those that remained and setting aside periods of the day when staff could work without being disturbed by messages.

C. Several large trials have taken place in recent years, involving companies from many sectors. In most of them, employees reported lower stress, better sleep and more time for family and exercise, and the majority of participating companies chose to continue with the shorter week once the trial ended. Some firms also found that fewer employees left their jobs, which saved the cost of recruiting and training new staff. Many participants said they used the extra day for household tasks, such as shopping and cleaning, which left the weekend free for rest and social life. Measures of business performance, such as revenue, generally stayed about the same during the trials, and in some companies they rose slightly. A minority of firms did return to the five-day week, often because some tasks could not be completed in less time or because customers expected staff to be available on every weekday.

D. Critics point out, however, that the trials have important limitations. The companies that took part were volunteers, so they may have been especially well suited to the change. In addition, many results were based on workers’ own descriptions of how they felt rather than on independent measures of output. A system that works in a small software company may not suit a hospital, a factory or a shop that must stay open six days a week. Others note that if employees try to fit five days of work into four, the extra pressure could eventually cause the very stress that the scheme was meant to reduce.

E. For such organisations, a four-day week often means a different arrangement rather than fewer hours for everyone. Some use rotas so that staff work four longer days while the business stays open as usual. Others reduce hours gradually or offer the shorter week only to certain departments. These solutions can work, but they require careful planning and may increase costs in the short term. In some countries, governments have tested shorter working weeks in parts of the public sector, such as local councils, where the challenge is to maintain services for residents who expect offices to be open throughout the week. Results from these schemes have been mixed, and they have often become the subject of political debate. Employers in these sectors also point out that hiring extra staff to cover the missing day can be difficult when there is already a shortage of qualified workers.

F. Whether the four-day week will become as common as the five-day week remains uncertain. Economists note that the earlier move to a shorter week happened over many decades and was linked to large increases in productivity. What seems clear is that the debate has encouraged many employers to think more carefully about how working time is used, and that may prove to be its most lasting effect. A century ago, many people worked six days a week, and the idea of a regular two-day weekend seemed unrealistic to many employers. It is possible that future generations will view the five-day week in the same way. Alternatively, the main change may be greater flexibility, with individual employees choosing different patterns of work rather than a single model for everyone.

Learning a language online used to mean watching recorded lessons alone at a computer. Today, many learners prefer live classes with a real teacher, even if the teacher is in another country. Some say the most important advantage is flexibility: lessons can be taken early in the morning or late at night, around work and family duties.

However, online learning is not suitable for everyone. Learners who find it difficult to organise their time often stop after a few weeks, especially when nobody checks whether they have done their homework. Teachers report that students who set a fixed time for lessons every week are far more likely to continue.

Another concern is speaking practice. In a large online group, each learner may speak for only a few minutes. For this reason, some schools now limit online groups to six students, while others offer extra conversation sessions with a partner. Many learners also use apps between lessons, although most teachers see these as a supplement rather than a replacement for real conversation.

A. For centuries, the Silk Road connected China with the Mediterranean, and cities such as Samarkand and Bukhara grew rich from the trade that passed through them. Merchants stopped in these cities to rest, exchange goods and find fresh animals for the next stage of the journey.

B. The routes carried far more than silk. Paper, spices, glass, metals and horses moved in both directions. Just as important were ideas: religions, scientific knowledge and artistic styles spread along the same roads as the goods.

C. Travel was slow and often dangerous. Caravans could take months to cross deserts and mountains, and they faced extreme heat, cold and the risk of attack. Caravanserais — inns built at regular distances along the routes — offered shelter and safety for travellers and their animals.

D. In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, the importance of the land routes declined. European traders increasingly used sea routes, which could carry larger loads more cheaply, and political changes made some parts of the land routes less secure.

E. Today, interest in the Silk Road has returned. Historic buildings in Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva attract visitors from all over the world, and many caravanserais have been restored. Tourism has become an important source of income for the region.

F. At the same time, new transport projects — railways, roads and pipelines — are once again linking Central Asia with China and Europe. Some writers describe these as a “new Silk Road”, although the goods they carry are very different from those of the past.

Many people believe that creativity is a rare talent that some people are born with and others are not. Psychologists, however, increasingly see it as a skill that can be developed with practice. Studies of successful artists and scientists show that they often produce a large number of ideas, most of which are never used. Quantity, it seems, is one of the routes to quality.

One factor that appears to help is a period of rest after hard work on a problem. People frequently report that a solution came to them while they were walking or taking a shower, rather than while they were sitting at a desk. Researchers believe that during such breaks the mind continues to work on the problem without our being aware of it.

Fear of criticism, on the other hand, seems to reduce creativity. When people expect their ideas to be judged harshly, they tend to suggest only safe and familiar solutions. For this reason, many organisations separate the stage of producing ideas from the stage of evaluating them.

Finally, creativity often grows from combining knowledge from different fields. An engineer who studies biology, or a designer who learns about psychology, may notice connections that specialists miss. This suggests that schools which encourage students to explore several subjects may be preparing them better for creative work.

The idea that the language we speak shapes the way we think has fascinated scholars for more than a century. In its strongest form, the claim is that speakers of different languages live in different mental worlds, unable to understand concepts for which their language has no words. Few researchers today accept this extreme position, not least because translation between languages, though imperfect, is clearly possible.

A weaker version of the idea, however, has received considerable support. Experiments suggest that language can influence what people notice and remember. For example, languages differ in how they describe the position of objects. Some rely on terms such as “left” and “right”, which depend on the speaker’s body, while others use fixed directions such as north and south. Speakers of the second type of language tend to remember the arrangement of objects in terms of those fixed directions, even in tasks that do not involve speaking.

Critics point out that such differences may be caused not by language itself but by the culture and environment in which the language is used. A community that lives in open landscape may need fixed directions for practical reasons, and the language simply reflects this need. Separating the effect of language from the effect of culture is therefore one of the central difficulties in this area of research.

Whatever the final answer, the debate has had practical consequences. It has encouraged researchers to study a wider range of languages, many of which are spoken by small communities and are at risk of disappearing. Each of these languages, linguists argue, represents a unique way of organising human experience, and its loss would be a loss to science as well as to its speakers.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good afternoon. Today I want to talk about urban gardens — small areas of land in cities where residents grow their own fruit and vegetables.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Although they are often seen as a modern trend, community gardens have a long history. During periods of food shortage in the twentieth century, many governments actually encouraged people to grow food in parks and empty plots.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Today the motivation is rather different. In a recent survey of garden members in three European cities, the most common reason given was not saving money, but meeting neighbours. Food production came only third, after improving mental health.

script.speaker: A
script.text: The environmental benefits are real but should not be exaggerated. Gardens absorb rainwater, which reduces the risk of flooding, and they provide habitats for insects such as bees. However, the amount of food they produce is small compared with the needs of a city.

script.speaker: A
script.text: One challenge is soil quality. Land in cities may contain metals from old industries, so many projects grow vegetables in raised beds filled with clean soil rather than directly in the ground.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Another challenge is security of tenure — in other words, how long a group can stay on the land. Many gardens are created on sites that are waiting for development, and after a few years the land is sold. Successful projects therefore try to sign long-term agreements with the city council.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Finally, research suggests that gardens work best when they are designed with local people rather than for them. Projects that involved residents from the planning stage had far more members after five years.

script.text: That sounds fine. How do I pay?

script.speaker: A
script.text: You can pay by card over the phone now, or in cash at reception before the first class.

script.speaker: B
script.text: I'll pay at reception, if that's all right.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Of course. Just one more thing: how did you hear about the course?

script.speaker: B
script.text: A friend told me about it, and then I saw the poster at the station.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Wonderful. I'll send you a confirmation by text message today. We look forward to seeing you.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Hartley Gardens. My name is Tom, and I'm one of the volunteers here. Before you set off, I'd like to give you a short introduction and a few practical details.

script.speaker: B
script.text: The gardens were created in 1902 by a local doctor, Edward Hartley, who believed that fresh air and plants were good for his patients. After his death, the house was turned into a school for a while, and the gardens were neglected. They were only restored in the 1990s, when a group of local residents raised the money to save them.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Today the gardens cover about twelve hectares. If you look at the map you were given, you'll see that the main path goes in a circle. If you follow it all the way round, it takes about an hour and a half, but there are several shorter routes as well.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Let me mention a few of the highlights. Just past the entrance, on your left, is the Rose Garden. It's at its best in June, so you've come at the right time. Beyond that is the lake. Please don't feed the ducks, because bread is actually bad for them.

script.speaker: B
script.text: On the far side of the lake you'll find the glasshouse, which contains tropical plants. It's kept very warm, so you may want to take off your coat before you go in. Next to it is the children's play area, which was rebuilt last year.

script.speaker: B
script.text: One of our newest features is the Sensory Garden, near the north gate. It was designed for visitors with poor eyesight, so all the plants were chosen for their smell or the way they feel when you touch them. Please do touch them; that's what they're there for.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Now, some practical information. The café is in the old stable building, and it's open until five. The toilets are next to the café and also by the main car park. If you need help, our volunteers are wearing green jackets.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Finally, there's a talk by our head gardener at three o'clock this afternoon in the education centre. It's about growing vegetables in small spaces, and it's free, but places are limited, so please collect a ticket from the information desk if you'd like to attend.

script.speaker: B
script.text: That's all from me. Enjoy your visit.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Hi, Daniel. Have you got a few minutes to talk about our presentation? It's only two weeks away now.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Sure, Emma. I've been reading about our topic, the four-day working week, and I think we've got plenty of material.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Good. I thought we could start with the trial that took place in Britain a few years ago. Most of the companies that took part decided to continue with the shorter week afterwards.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Yes, but I think we should be careful there. The companies chose to take part, so they were probably more enthusiastic than average. That might make the results look better than they would be in general.

script.speaker: C
script.text: That's a good point. We should mention it as a limitation.

script.speaker: D
script.text: What surprised me was that productivity didn't fall in most of the companies. I expected it to drop at least a little.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Me too. Apparently people cut down on long meetings and wasted time. One manager said meetings were reduced to thirty minutes.

script.speaker: D
script.text: And the staff reported less stress and better sleep. Although those results came from questionnaires, so they depend on what people said about themselves.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Right. Now, how should we divide the work? I'd be happy to do the background and the history of working hours.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Then I'll take the results of the trial. And maybe we can both do the conclusion together?

script.speaker: C
script.text: Fine. What about visuals? Our tutor said she wanted fewer slides with words and more charts.

script.speaker: D
script.text: I can make the charts. I'm better with spreadsheets than you are, I think.

script.speaker: C
script.text: That's true! I'll find a short video clip, then. Something from an interview with an employee, maybe. Not more than a minute, though.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Good idea. One thing I'm worried about is the question time at the end. Some people are bound to ask whether this would work in hospitals or schools.

script.speaker: C
script.text: We should prepare an answer to that. The trial was mainly in offices, so we can say the evidence for other sectors is still limited.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Agreed. When shall we practise?

script.speaker: C
script.text: How about next Wednesday afternoon in the library? We could book one of the study rooms.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Wednesday's fine, but the library rooms are always busy. Let's use the empty classroom on the second floor instead.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Perfect. I'll send you my part by Monday so you can read it first.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Good morning. Today I'm going to talk about honeybees, and in particular about how they communicate. For a long time, people wondered how bees that had found a good source of food were able to direct other bees to it. The answer came from the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch, who studied bees for many years and later received a Nobel Prize for his work.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Von Frisch discovered that a bee returning to the hive performs a kind of dance on the surface of the honeycomb. When the food is close to the hive, the bee moves in small circles. This is called the round dance, and it simply tells the other bees that food is nearby.

script.speaker: A
script.text: When the food is further away, the bee performs what is known as the waggle dance. It runs forward in a straight line while shaking its body from side to side, then circles back and repeats the movement. The direction of the straight run shows the direction of the food in relation to the sun, and the length of the waggle tells the other bees the distance they need to fly.

script.speaker: A
script.text: What is remarkable is that the hive is usually dark, so the other bees cannot see the dance clearly. Instead, they follow the dancer closely and pick up the information through touch and vibration. They also learn the smell of the flowers from the dancer's body.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Of course, not every scientist accepted these findings at first. Some argued that bees simply followed the scent of the food. It was only later, when researchers used radar to track individual bees, that it became clear that the bees really did fly in the direction indicated by the dance.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Why does this matter today? Bees are responsible for pollinating a large proportion of the crops we eat, and in many regions bee populations have declined. Several causes have been suggested, including disease, the loss of wild flowers and the use of certain chemicals on farms.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Understanding how bees communicate can help farmers and planners. For example, if we know how far bees are prepared to fly, we can decide where to plant strips of flowers so that bees can reach them easily. In some cities, people are now encouraged to plant flowers on balconies and roofs.

script.speaker: A
script.text: In our next lecture, we'll look at how bees choose a new home when a colony becomes too large, a process in which, interestingly, the dance also plays a central role.

script.text: Not this one, I'm afraid. You need the number forty-two. It leaves from the stop across the road every twenty minutes.

script.speaker: D

script.speaker: C
script.text: It's actually twenty per cent cheaper this weekend. The sale starts on Saturday.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Welcome to the Riverside Summer Festival. Here is some information to help you enjoy your day. The festival runs from ten in the morning until eleven at night. The main stage is in the centre of the park, and the first concert begins at two o'clock.

script.speaker: B
script.text: If you're interested in food, the market is next to the lake, where you can try dishes from more than twenty countries. Please remember that the festival is plastic-free, so bring your own bottle. Water is free at the fountains near each entrance.

script.speaker: B
script.text: For families, there's a children's area beside the north gate, with games and face painting. Children under twelve must be with an adult at all times. If you lose your group, go to the information tent, which is the large blue tent next to the main stage.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Finally, the festival ends with fireworks over the lake at ten thirty. The last buses back to the city centre leave at eleven fifteen, so please plan your journey home.

script.speaker: C
script.text: So, Bek, we need to choose a topic for our group project in economics. Any ideas?

script.speaker: D
script.text: I was thinking about small family businesses in our city. My uncle runs a bakery, so we could interview him.

script.speaker: C
script.text: That's a nice idea, but our teacher said the project should include data, not only interviews. Could we get numbers from your uncle?

script.speaker: D
script.text: He keeps records of his sales, and I think he'd share them if we don't publish his name.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Good. We could compare his sales before and after he started selling online. That would be interesting.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Agreed. He started online orders about two years ago. He says it was difficult at first because he had to learn to take good photos of the bread.

script.speaker: C
script.text: Ha! How about the presentation? I'm not very confident speaking in front of the class.

script.speaker: D
script.text: Then you could prepare the charts, and I'll present. But you should say at least one part, because the teacher gives marks to each person.

script.speaker: C
script.text: OK, I'll present the conclusion. That's the shortest part. When is the deadline again?

script.speaker: D
script.text: The twentieth of May. Let's aim to finish a week earlier, so we have time to practise.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Today on 'Working Lives' I'm talking to Daniel, who left his job in a bank to become a mountain guide. Daniel, why did you make such a big change?

script.speaker: D
script.text: Honestly, I was bored. The salary was good, but I spent all day in an office looking at numbers. At weekends I always went hiking, and one day I realised I was only really happy on Saturdays and Sundays.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Was it difficult to start?

script.speaker: D
script.text: Very. I needed a qualification, which took almost a year, and during that time I had almost no income. My family was worried, especially my father, who thought I was making a mistake.

script.speaker: A
script.text: And now?

script.speaker: D
script.text: Now he comes on some of my tours! He's changed his mind completely.

script.speaker: A
script.text: What's the hardest part of the job?

script.speaker: D
script.text: The weather. You have to make decisions quickly. If a storm is coming, you must turn back, even if the group is disappointed. Safety always comes first.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Do you earn as much as before?

script.speaker: D
script.text: No, less, maybe half in a bad year. But I spend less too, and I'm much healthier.

script.speaker: A
script.text: What advice would you give to people who want to change careers?

script.speaker: D
script.text: Try the new work part-time first, if you can. I guided small groups at weekends for a year before I left the bank. That way I knew I really enjoyed it.

script.speaker: A
script.text: In today's lecture I want to look at the history of tea, one of the most widely drunk beverages in the world. Tea originated in China, where it was first used as a medicine before it became an everyday drink.

script.speaker: A
script.text: From China, tea spread to Japan, where a formal tea ceremony developed, and later along trade routes to Central Asia, India and Europe. In Central Asia, tea became an important part of hospitality: offering tea to a guest is still a sign of respect.

script.speaker: A
script.text: In Europe, tea arrived in the seventeenth century. At first it was very expensive, so only wealthy families could afford it. It was often kept in locked boxes to prevent servants from taking it.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Over time, prices fell, largely because of large plantations established in India and later in Sri Lanka. By the nineteenth century, tea had become a drink for all social classes in Britain.

script.speaker: A
script.text: The way tea is prepared varies a great deal. In some countries it is served with milk, in others with sugar, lemon or even salt. Green tea, which is not fermented, remains especially popular in East Asia and in parts of Central Asia.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Next week we'll discuss coffee, and compare how the two drinks influenced trade and social life.
